candidate.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity, printed p.10: provide care and education for acute/chronic psychosocial health issues; assess coping; promote therapeutic environment; use therapeutic communication and behavioral-management techniques.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — body dysmorphic disorder recognition
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize body dysmorphic disorder by the combination of preoccupation with slight or unobservable appearance flaws, repetitive appearance-related behaviors, and clinically significant distress or impairment.

options.A: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, when obsessions and compulsions are present but are not centered on perceived appearance defects.
options.B: Social anxiety disorder, when fear of scrutiny or embarrassment is primary without a persistent perceived appearance flaw.
options.C: Illness anxiety disorder, when fear of having or acquiring serious disease is primary rather than perceived appearance defects.
options.D: Body dysmorphic disorder, characterized by preoccupation with slight or unobservable appearance flaws plus repetitive appearance-related behaviors and clinically significant impairment.

candidate.rationale: StatPearls summarizes DSM-5-TR body dysmorphic disorder as preoccupation with one or more perceived physical defects that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, or reassurance seeking, with clinically significant distress or impairment. D directly matches this pattern.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Body dysmorphic disorder is characterized by preoccupation with slight/unobservable perceived appearance defects plus repetitive appearance-related behaviors and clinically significant distress or impairment.
candidate.source_locator: Introduction; History and Physical; Evaluation > Body Dysmorphic Disorder DSM-5-TR Criteria: perceived defects/flaws not observable or slight to others; repetitive behaviors; clinically significant distress or impairment; appearance concern not better explained by eating disorder.
